front: What does a **hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell** do?
back: It uses hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity; water is the only chemical product.

front: Overall reaction in a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell
Energy change in a fuel cell
back: Chemical energy to electrical energy (the hydrogen is not burnt).

front: Fuel cell or battery: which is recharged?
back: A battery is recharged. A fuel cell keeps working as long as hydrogen and oxygen are supplied.

front: Main environmental advantage of fuel-cell vehicles
back: Only water is emitted: no CO₂, CO, particulates or oxides of nitrogen from the vehicle.

front: Two other advantages of fuel cells over petrol engines
back: More efficient (more useful energy from the fuel) and quieter, with fewer moving parts.

front: Why is hydrogen hard to use as a vehicle fuel?
back: It is a gas: it needs large, strong high-pressure tanks and is highly flammable.

front: Where does most hydrogen come from?
back: Methane (natural gas), which releases CO₂; electrolysis needs a lot of electricity.

front: Two practical drawbacks of fuel-cell cars
back: Few hydrogen filling stations; fuel cells are expensive (platinum catalysts).

front: Mass of water from 1 kg of hydrogen in a fuel cell
back: 9 kg (4 g of H₂ gives 36 g of H₂O).
